newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Cyprus talks to end Saturday with agreed principles.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus talks to end Saturday with agreed principles.

text.p: Talks between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities are expected to end on Saturday, a day earlier than scheduled, with a joint statement detailing principles agreed upon so far, sources close to the negotiations said on Friday.

President Glafcos Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash have been meeting since Wednesday at a rural resort north of New York city to try to revive negotiations aimed at reuniting their divided island as a bi-zonal, bi-communal federation.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan's special adviser for Cyprus, former Ecuadorean Foreign Minister Diego Cordovez, has held separate and joint meetings with the two leaders. They also have met alone, sometimes taking walks together on the picturesque estate called Troutbeck, 90 miles (145 kms) from New York.

One source said that on their return to Nicosia, U.N. resident representative Gustave Feissel would hold "proximity talks," shuttling between Clerides and Denktash. Another round of direct talks will take place in Switzerland in August.

The proposed joint statement would commit the two sides to pursuing "a continuing and sustained process of open-ended direct negotiations" under U.N. auspices aimed at reaching a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus problem.
Cyprus has been virtually partitioned since troops from Turkey took over the north of the island in 1974 in reaction to a coup in Nicosia backed by the junta then ruling Greece.

The statement says a comprehensive settlement would "comprise a new constitution, legal instruments containing agreements on territorial adjustments, on security arrangements, on arrangements relating to displaced persons and property rights."
Other legal instruments might deal with referenda to be held by each community to approve the new federal constitution and on the entry into force and implementation of the comprhensive settlement.
The joint statement, still subject to amendment, echoes many of the principles on which past attempts to fashion a federal solution have been based.

The state of Cyprus would have "a single sovereignty and international personality and a single citizenship, with its independence and territorial integrity safeguarded." The settlement would exclude union of Cyprus in whole or in part with any other country or any form of partition or secession.

A key paragraph says: "The bi-communal and bi-zonal federation shall be established freely by the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot communities. All powers not vested by them in the federal government shall rest with the two federated states."

The federal republic "shall be one territory composed of two politically equal federated states" and shall have "one sovereignty which is indivisible and which emanates equally from the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities. One community cannot claim sovereignty over the other community."

Political equality would not mean equal numerical participation in all branches and administration of the federal government. It would be reflected in the fact that the approval and amendment of the federal constitution would require the approval of both communities and in the effective participation of both in all organs and decisions of the federal government.
The federal constitution would safeguard the identity, integrity and security of each community as well as its political economic, social, cultural, linguistic and religious rights.

One source said the generally good atmosphere surrounding the talks was somewhat spoiled on Friday by a press report that the European Commission in Brussels had agreed in principle to open membership talks with six countries, including Cyprus.
The Turkish Cypriots strongly oppose any negotiations on membership by the current Greek Cypriot-led government, which they do not recognise and say cannot speak on their behalf.
